introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography, Paper 3 (0750), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three and a quarter hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer ALL THE THREE QUESTIONS. Question ONE carries THIRTY-FOUR marks and the rest carry THIRTY-THREE marks each.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answer.

Calculators are allowed.

Materials required: Topographic map, Graph Paper and photograph.

questions.enonce_markdown: EITHER a) Locate the area where the fieldwork was carried out **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**How to use this model answer.** The questions ask about the candidate's OWN fieldwork, so no single answer exists. The model below is written for the topic **i) Variation in a soil characteristic: soil moisture content down a slope** (a study of one hillside farm field in Cameroon). All names and numbers are ILLUSTRATIVE: replace them by your own. The same plan works for the other topics (weather element, vegetation, land use, farm location, factory characteristics).

**Location (5 marks).** Give the answer in two parts.
1. *Written location (about 2 marks):* the name of the site (for example "the hillside farm field at Village X"), the nearest town or village, the Sub-division, Division and Region, its position in relation to a well-known feature (road, school, river), the approximate latitude and longitude or the grid reference on the topographic map, and the length of the slope studied (for example 120 m from the crest to the valley floor).
2. *Sketch map (about 3 marks):* a neat map with a frame, title, north arrow, scale and key, showing the slope and the transect line from the crest to the foot, the five sampling stations (Station 1 to Station 5, equally spaced), the road, the stream or valley floor, the land use around (farms, trees, houses) and the contours or arrows showing the slope direction. An inset map of Cameroon showing the Region earns extra credit.

questions.enonce_markdown: b) State your objective and hypothesis **(4 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Objective and hypothesis (4 marks).**
- *Aim/objective (2 marks):* to find out how soil moisture content varies from the top to the bottom of a slope, and to explain the variation.
- *Hypothesis (2 marks):* "Soil moisture content increases from the crest to the foot of the slope." A null hypothesis may be added: "There is no relationship between the position on the slope and the soil moisture content." A hypothesis must be testable, so it names the two variables (position on the slope, moisture content) and the expected direction.

questions.enonce_markdown: c) i) What type of data were needed to test the hypothesis? **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(c)(i) Types of data needed to test the hypothesis (3 marks).**
- *Primary data (collected in the field):* the soil moisture content at each station (mass of the wet sample and mass of the dry sample), the slope angle between stations, the distance of each station from the crest, and field notes on the soil colour, texture, depth, vegetation cover and land use around the sample.
- *Secondary data (from existing sources):* the topographic map of the area (height and slope), the rainfall records of the nearest weather station for the week of the study, and the soil map or reports of the Region.

questions.enonce_markdown: ii) How were the data collected? **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(c)(ii) How the data were collected (5 marks).**
1. *Sampling design:* a systematic transect from the crest to the foot, with five stations at equal intervals (every 25 m along the measured slope), which covers every part of the slope. At each station three samples were taken a few metres apart, to reduce chance errors.
2. *Equipment:* measuring tape (50 m) and ranging poles, clinometer (or a homemade one) for the slope angle, soil auger or trowel, labelled polythene bags, a sensitive scale, baking trays and an oven or the sun for drying, a notebook, a camera and a GPS or map.
3. *Procedure:* at each station the surface litter was removed and a 10 cm-deep sample was dug out, put at once into a labelled airtight bag, and weighed (wet mass). In the school laboratory the sample was dried (oven at about 105 degrees C, or sun-dried until the mass stopped changing) and weighed again (dry mass). Moisture content (%) = (wet mass - dry mass) / dry mass x 100.
4. *Other measurements:* the slope angle between stations (clinometer and ranging poles), soil colour (Munsell-type chart or comparison), depth of the soil (auger), and a sketch of the slope.
5. *Care:* all the samples were taken on the same morning, on a day without rain in the previous two days, to give comparable results; the group shared the tasks (measurers, recorders, samplers).

questions.enonce_markdown: d) State the results obtained **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(d) Results obtained (3 marks).** (ILLUSTRATIVE values: use your own.)

| Station | Position | Distance from crest (m) | Mean moisture content (%) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Crest | 0 | 14 |
| 2 | Upper slope | 25 | 18 |
| 3 | Mid slope | 50 | 23 |
| 4 | Lower slope | 75 | 27 |
| 5 | Foot of slope | 100 | 33 |

The moisture content rose steadily from about 14 % at the crest to about 33 % at the foot, which is more than double (1 mark for the table or description, 1 mark for the trend, 1 mark for the figures quoted). The results were presented as a table, a line graph of moisture against distance, and a slope profile with the moisture values written at each station; a statistical test (for example Spearman's rank coefficient between distance and moisture) shows a strong positive correlation, which supports the hypothesis.

questions.enonce_markdown: e) What possibly accounts for the results obtained? **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(e) What accounts for the results obtained (3 marks).** (Explain the result you obtained; for the illustrative result above:)
- Water drains downslope under gravity, by overland flow and throughflow, so the foot of the slope receives water from the whole slope and stays wetter (1 mark).
- The soil at the foot is deeper, finer-textured (more clay and silt, carried down by erosion) and richer in organic matter, so it holds more water, while the crest has thin, coarse, well-drained soil (1 mark).
- The crest is more exposed to sun and wind, so evaporation is higher; the foot is nearer the water table or the stream and is shaded by vegetation (1 mark).
Mention also that a steep slope increases run-off and reduces infiltration.

questions.enonce_markdown: f) How were the difficulties encountered during the fieldwork overcome? **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(f) Difficulties and how they were overcome (5 marks).** Any five (1 mark per difficulty and its remedy):
1. *Rain interrupted the fieldwork and made the soil wetter:* the date was changed and the sampling was done on a dry morning, two days after the last rain.
2. *Access to the farm field was restricted:* the owner and the village head were informed and gave permission before the visit.
3. *The slope was steep and slippery, and the equipment was heavy:* the group worked in pairs, wore strong shoes and shared the equipment.
4. *Limited time and the sample differences from one spot to another:* the pilot survey fixed the number of stations and three samples were taken at each station to reduce errors.
5. *No oven available at school:* the samples were dried in the sun on trays, and weighed repeatedly until the mass was constant.
6. *Errors in the measure of the slope angle and in the reading of the scale:* the readings were repeated and the mean was used.

questions.enonce_markdown: g) Of what importance was the fieldwork? **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(g) Importance of the fieldwork (5 marks).** Any five points (1 mark each):
1. It gives first-hand (primary) data, so the results are reliable and relevant to the local area.
2. It allows the hypothesis to be tested and the theory taught in class (soil catena, drainage) to be checked in the real world.
3. It develops practical skills: sampling, measuring, recording, data presentation, analysis and report writing.
4. It develops teamwork, planning and communication.
5. It gives information that can help farmers and planners: where to grow crops that need much water, where erosion and waterlogging are likely, how to conserve the soil.
6. It makes the subject interesting and improves the understanding and memory of the concepts, and it prepares for higher studies and careers (agriculture, environment, planning).
7. It raises awareness of the environment and the need to protect the soil.

questions.enonce_markdown: OR a) i) State the topic and the duration of the study **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**How to use this model answer.** The questions ask about the candidate's OWN project-based study, so no single answer exists. The model below is written for a project on **access to safe drinking water in a rural community**. All names and numbers are ILLUSTRATIVE: replace them by your own project.

**(a)(i) Topic and duration (3 marks).** Topic: "Access to safe drinking water in Village X (a rural community in the ... Region): sources, distance and quality" (2 marks). Duration: for example three weeks in total, made up of one week of planning, four days of fieldwork and one week for analysis and writing the report (1 mark).

questions.enonce_markdown: ii) Locate the area of study **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown: **(a)(ii) Location of the area of study (5 marks).** Give a written location (the village, Sub-division, Division and Region; distance and direction from the nearest town; the main road or river nearby; latitude and longitude or grid reference) for about 2 marks, and a neat sketch map for about 3 marks, with a frame, title, north arrow, scale and key, showing the village boundary, the main road, the houses, the water sources (spring, stream, borehole, well, stand taps), the relief or the stream, and an inset map of Cameroon.

questions.enonce_markdown: b) Describe the problem identified which necessitated the investigation **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown: **(b) The problem identified (3 marks).** The people of Village X have not enough safe water close to their homes. Many households walk about 30 to 45 minutes to a spring or a stream, mainly women and children, who lose time for school and work; the sources are unprotected and polluted by animals and run-off; the flow falls in the dry season; the stand taps built earlier no longer work. As a result, water-borne diseases (diarrhoea, typhoid) are frequent, which needed an investigation (names of the problem 1 mark, its causes 1 mark, its consequences 1 mark). The figures here are illustrative.

questions.enonce_markdown: c) i) State the objective and expected outcome which guided your investigation **(2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(c)(i) Objective and expected outcome (2 marks).**
- *Objective (1 mark):* to find out where the households of Village X get their water, how far and how long they walk, and how safe the sources are, in order to propose ways of improving water supply.
- *Expected outcome (1 mark):* to show that most households depend on unprotected sources far from their homes, and to suggest realistic ways of improving the supply.

questions.enonce_markdown: ii) Describe the materials used and method of investigation **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(c)(ii) Materials used and method of investigation (5 marks).**
- *Materials (2 marks):* questionnaire forms and clipboards, a tape or a pedometer/GPS to measure distances, a stopwatch, a measuring jug or bucket to estimate the water carried, sample bottles and a simple turbidity (clear-water) test or a test kit if available, a camera, a topographic map or sketch map of the village.
- *Method (3 marks):* a pilot test of the questionnaire with five households; a systematic sample of every fifth household from a list of houses (for example 50 of about 250 households); interviews with the village head and the water committee; observation and counting of people at the main sources at peak times; measurement of the distance and the walking time from the houses to the source; photographs of the sources and of their state.

questions.enonce_markdown: d) i) How was the data collected, analysed and presented? **(5 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(d)(i) Collection, analysis and presentation of the data (5 marks).**
- *Collection (2 marks):* primary data by questionnaire and interviews (source used, quantity of water, time spent, treatment, illnesses), observation and measurement at the sources; secondary data from the council, the health centre records and the topographic map.
- *Analysis (1.5 marks):* tally and percentage of households by source used; mean, median and range of the time and the distance; comparison of the wet season and the dry season; a correlation (for example Spearman's rank) between the distance to the source and the quantity of water used per person.
- *Presentation (1.5 marks):* tables, a bar graph or pie chart of the sources used, a histogram or line graph of walking times, a dot or proportional-symbol map of the sources and the households, and annotated photographs, with titles and key.

questions.enonce_markdown: ii) What was or were your result (s)? **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown: **(d)(ii) The results (3 marks).** (ILLUSTRATIVE: use your own.) About 60 % of the 50 households used unprotected springs or streams, 25 % used a borehole or a protected well and 15 % used stand taps or rainwater; the mean round trip to the source was about 35 minutes, and the water carried was about 10 litres per person per day, below the recommended amount; two out of five households reported diarrhoea in the previous month. The distance to the source increased with the distance of the house from the village centre, and the supply fell sharply in the dry season (1 mark for the main result, 1 for figures, 1 for the pattern or the link between the variables).

questions.enonce_markdown: e) Suggest ways by which the problem identified can be addressed. **(4 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(e) Ways by which the problem can be addressed (4 marks).** Any four (1 mark each, stated and explained):
1. Protect the springs (a concrete spring box, fencing and drainage) so that the water is not polluted.
2. Drill boreholes with hand pumps, or build a gravity-fed water scheme with stand taps, in partnership with the council, the Ministry or NGOs.
3. Collect rainwater from roofs in tanks to increase the supply, especially in the wet season.
4. Create and train a village water committee to maintain the points, collect small fees and repair the pumps quickly.
5. Educate the people on water treatment (boiling, chlorination), hygiene and the care of the sources.
6. Plant trees and protect the catchment of the springs to keep the flow constant.

questions.enonce_markdown: f) State the challenges encountered during the investigation and explain the measures used to overcome them. **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(f) Challenges and the measures used to overcome them (3 marks).** Any three (1 mark each, challenge + measure):
- Some people were reluctant to answer, or were absent: the village head introduced the team and the visits were made in the evening.
- The language barrier: a local interpreter was used and the questionnaire was translated.
- Rain and bad roads delayed the work: the schedule was made flexible and the team worked in pairs.
- Inaccurate answers about quantities and times: the answers were checked by direct measurement and observation at the sources.
- Limited time and equipment: the sample was reduced to a manageable number, chosen systematically, and the work was divided among the group members.
